Which patient scenario represents the most appropriate indication for eccentric anterior glenoid reaming during shoulder surgery?
Answer Choices: (A) 70-year-old male with glenoid retroversion of 18-degrees undergoing shoulder arthroplasty (B) 70-year-old female with humeral anteversion of 13-degrees undergoing shoulder arthroplasty (C) 63-year-old female with glenoid retroversion of 22-degrees and mild posterior wear undergoing shoulder arthroplasty (D) 65-year-old female with glenoid retroversion of 25-degrees undergoing shoulder arthroplasty (E) 65-year-old female with a glenoid retroversion of 13-degrees undergoing shoulder arthroplasty (F) 68-year-old female with glenoid retroversion of 20-degrees undergoing reverse shoulder arthroplasty (G) 72-year-old male with glenoid retroversion of 15-degrees undergoing shoulder arthroplasty (H) 65-year-old female with glenoid retroversion of 30-degrees and severe posterior wear undergoing shoulder arthroplasty (I) 58-year-old male with glenoid retroversion of 12-degrees undergoing shoulder arthroplasty (J) 55-year-old male with glenoid retroversion of 8-degrees undergoing total shoulder arthroplasty

The best indication for **eccentric anterior glenoid reaming** is **mild posterior glenoid wear with retroversion of approximately ≤10–15°**, where adequate native bone stock can be preserved.

- **Accepted maximum correction:** about **15° of glenoid retroversion**.  
- Beyond this, eccentric reaming removes excessive anterior/inferior bone and causes unacceptable **joint-line medialization** and loss of glenoid bone support.
- **Mild posterior wear:** appropriate for eccentric reaming.
- **Severe posterior wear:** not appropriate for eccentric reaming alone; consider a posteriorly augmented component, bone grafting, custom reconstruction, or reverse shoulder arthroplasty depending on cuff status and bone loss.

### Degree comparison

| Retroversion | Eccentric reaming alone |
|---:|---|
| **13°** | Generally acceptable, though near the upper limit |
| **18°** | Usually excessive; not preferred |
| **20°** | Excessive; use an alternative corrective strategy |
| **22°** | Not appropriate |
| **25°** | Not appropriate; severe deformity |
| **30°** | Clearly not appropriate |

Thus, among typical A–J choices, select the option describing **mild posterior glenoid erosion/retroversion no greater than approximately 15°**—most likely the **13° case**, not the 18–30° cases. The exact A–J mapping cannot be assigned because the option text was not included.

Eccentric anterior glenoid reaming is best suited for correcting **limited glenoid retroversion—generally up to about 10–15°**—while preserving adequate bone stock. Retroversion ≥18° or severe posterior wear typically requires augmented components, bone grafting, or another reconstruction strategy.

The best choice is the 65-year-old woman with **13° of glenoid retroversion** undergoing shoulder arthroplasty.

FINAL ANSWER: E
